title: PostgreSQL Trigger Fundamentals
description: Understand trigger mechanics, Row vs Statement level triggers, and the NEW and OLD pseudo-records.

data.text: A **Trigger** is a database callback function that executes automatically whenever a specified event (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, or `TRUNCATE`) occurs on a table or view.

rows: Executes once for every row affected by the statement
Executes exactly once per SQL command regardless of rows affected
Cannot access individual row data; uses transition tables.

data.text: A Complete Trigger Function and Registration

Creating a trigger is a two-step process: write a function that returns `trigger`, then register it with `CREATE TRIGGER` on a table. The function must return `NEW` for `BEFORE` row triggers, `OLD` for `DELETE`, or `NULL` to cancel the operation.

data.title: Write the function, then attach the trigger
data.content: The function stamps `updated_at` on every update; the trigger fires once per modified row.

data.title: Interview angle: triggers hide logic
data.text: Triggers are powerful but they move behavior out of the application and into the schema, where it is invisible during code review and harder to test and debug. Interviewers often ask when you would avoid them. Good answers: when the logic is business-critical and must be versioned with the application, when a trigger fires once per row on a huge batch update, or when the same effect can be achieved with a constraint or a generated column. Use triggers for auditing, normalization, and integrity checks that must hold for every writer, including ad-hoc SQL.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Triggers execute automatically upon database DML events.
Row-level triggers use `FOR EACH ROW` and access `NEW` and `OLD` records.
Triggers must execute a trigger function returning `TRIGGER`.
